Welcome toMonitor at the Door

A monitor catches 99% of sources. When its alarm sounds, how likely is a source?

How would you like to begin?

Listen to the intro

About: Bayes's theorem on a crowd: P(R|G) against P(G|R) for a radiation monitor

About this simulation

On screen
Left: the corridor seen from above, with the monitor arch in the door at its centre. People walk through from left to right, carriers of a source wear a small yellow badge, the arch flashes red for every alarm, and people who set it off keep a red ring. Beneath the door, one bar of fixed full width holds all the alarms so far: red for alarms from people with a source, grey for alarms from people without one. Right: the fraction of alarms from a source against the fraction of the crowd that has passed, with the four previous runs in pale grey and, once a run ends, a dashed line at the Bayes value P(R | G). Legends above the corridor and beneath the graph name each mark.
Controls
r is the fraction of people carrying a source, η1 the probability the alarm sounds for a carrier, η0 the background false-alarm probability for everyone else, and the crowd size is 100, 1000 or 10 000. Any change stops and clears the current run; changing r, η1 or η0 also clears the grey curves of earlier runs. Run the crowd sends a fresh, independently drawn crowd through the door in about ten seconds.
Measured
Every person gets two draws from a seeded random generator: carrier if the first is below r, then alarm if the second is below η1 (carrier) or η0 (no source). All counts are exact tallies of the people who have passed; at 1000 and 10 000 people only a representative sample of figures is drawn.

Guided Inquiry

1 · When the alarm sounds

Set r = 0.01, η1 = 0.99, η0 = 0.05 and a crowd of 1000. Before pressing Run the crowd, predict roughly what fraction of the people who set off the alarm will be carrying a source.

2 · Small crowds, big crowds

Keep r = 0.01, η1 = 0.99 and η0 = 0.05, and set the crowd to 100. Run the crowd several times, then set the crowd to 10 000. Before running the larger crowd several times, predict how the fraction of alarms from a source behaves.

3 · A perfect detector

Keep r = 0.01, η0 = 0.05 and the crowd of 10 000, and raise the detection probability from η1 = 0.99 to 1.00, a perfect detector. Before running the crowd, predict the fraction of alarms from a source. When the run ends, compare the dashed Bayes line with the 0.167 it marked at η1 = 0.99. The run’s own fraction scatters by about 0.015 from crowd to crowd.

4 · A quieter background

Keep r = 0.01 and the crowd of 10 000, set η1 back to 0.99, and lower the background false-alarm probability from η0 = 0.05 to 0.01. Before running the crowd, predict the fraction of alarms from a source.

5 · Common sources

Keep η1 = 0.99, η0 = 0.01 and the crowd of 10 000, and raise the fraction carrying a source from r = 0.01 to 0.2. Before running the crowd, predict the fraction of alarms from a source.

6 · Why the base rate matters

Bayes’s theorem gives P(R | G) = η1r / [η1r + η0(1 − r)]. A detector that almost never misses (η1 ≈ 1) still gives mostly false alarms when carriers are rare, because the small false-alarm rate η0 acts on the large majority who carry nothing.

P(G | R) and P(R | G) are different numbers. Perfecting η1 barely helps; lowering η0, or screening a group in which sources are common, transforms the answer. A larger crowd only sharpens the estimate of P(R | G), it never changes its value.

01

At a glance

This sim sends a crowd through a monitor arch at a laboratory door. A fraction r of the people carry a radioactive source. The arch sounds with probability η1 for a carrier and with probability η0 for everyone else, so some alarms are true and some are false. The sim counts the alarms and follows the fraction of them that came from a source.

What you'll learn

  • What the two probabilities η1 and η0 each describe.
  • What fixes the fraction of alarms that come from a source.
  • Why that fraction wobbles from run to run, and what the crowd size does to the wobble.
The set-up in the sim, sketched: the corridor seen from above, the arch in the door, people walking left to right, a yellow badge on each carrier, and the bar beneath the door that holds the alarms.

What's on screen

  • The corridor. A yellow badge means the person carries a source. A red ring marks a person who set off the alarm.
  • The bar beneath the door holds every alarm so far: red for alarms from people with a source, grey for alarms from people without one.
  • The graph is the fraction of alarms from a source against the fraction of the crowd that has passed. Earlier runs stay in pale grey, and a dashed line appears when a run ends.
  • The readouts: people passed, all alarms, from a source, no source (false) and fraction from a source.
See itLook at the opening state, before any crowd has been sent through. Watch for: people passed reading 0 / 1000 and all alarms reading 0.

03

The share of alarms from a source is η1r over η1r + η0(1 − r)

Let R be a person who carries a source, with P(R) = r, and G the alarm, so P(G | R) = η1. The share of alarms from a source is the reverse conditional probability, P(R | G) (notes 8.6):

An alarm comes from a carrier or from a person with no source, never both:

Together they give (notes 8.7)

At r = 0.01, η1 = 0.99 and η0 = 0.05, a crowd of 1000 holds about 10 carriers, who set off 0.99 × 10 = 9.9 alarms. The other 990 people set off 0.05 × 990 = 49.5. Of 59.4 alarms, 9.9 are from a source: P(R | G) = 0.167, one in six.

The expected alarms in 1000 people at the opening settings. Red is from a source, grey from none.
r η1 η0 N

These move the sim's controls too. The values are the expected ones.

Key idea. The arch's accuracy, η1, is P(G | R). The fraction of alarms from a source is P(R | G), and the false-alarm term η0(1 − r) is part of it.
See itSend a crowd of 1000 through at the opening settings. Watch for: people passed reading 1000 / 1000, all alarms 60, from a source 10, no source (false) 50, and fraction from a source 0.167. This is one fixed draw, so your own run will differ a little.
04

A bigger crowd narrows the scatter of the fraction but does not move its target

P(R | G) belongs to r, η1 and η0 alone. The crowd size N enters only through the number of alarms, A = N[η1r + η0(1 − r)], which is 59.4 for N = 1000. Given A alarms, each is from a source independently with probability P(R | G), so the number from a source is binomial (notes 8.3):

n trials, each a success with probability q. Here n = A and q = P(R | G).

Dividing by A, the fraction at the end of a crowd has the standard deviation

The fraction at the end of a crowd, one standard deviation either side of 0.167, for the three crowd sizes.

For the two larger crowds about two-thirds of runs end within one σf of 0.167 (notes 8.4). A crowd of 100 sets off only about six alarms and A itself varies, so a run can end anywhere from 0 to above 0.3.

Key idea. A bigger crowd tightens the fraction around P(R | G), as 1/√A. It does not move the value it settles at.
See itSend a crowd of 100 through, with the opening r, η1 and η0. Watch for: people passed reading 100 / 100, all alarms 5, from a source 1, and fraction from a source 0.200. Another draw can read anywhere from 0 to above 0.3.
See itNow send a crowd of 10 000 through. Watch for: people passed reading 10000 / 10000, all alarms 584, from a source 99, no source (false) 485, and fraction from a source 0.170.
05

A perfect detector raises the share of alarms from a source only from 0.167 to 0.168

Raising η1 from 0.99 to 1.00 catches the one carrier in a hundred that the arch used to miss. In 10 000 people that is about one more true alarm, 99 becoming 100. The 495 false alarms come from the 9900 people with no source, and η1 does not touch them. They still outnumber the true alarms about five to one, so P(R | G) rises only to 0.168.

The alarms in 10 000 people at r = 0.01 and η0 = 0.05, for η1 = 0.99 and η1 = 1.00.

P(G | R) = 1 says that every carrier sets off the alarm. It says nothing about how many other people do, and the alarm's meaning depends on both.

Go deeper: a second passage

Suppose the person who set off the alarm walks through again and it sounds again, the two alarms being independent for a given person (notes 8.1, problem 1). Then

At the opening settings it is 0.0098/(0.0098 + 0.0025 × 0.99) = 0.798, larger than 0.167 whenever η1 > η0.

Key idea. Missing fewer carriers cannot cure false alarms. Only a lower η0 or a higher r can.
See itSet η1 to 1.00 and send a crowd of 10 000 through. Watch for: from a source reading 100, no source (false) reading 485, and fraction from a source 0.171, close to the dashed line at 0.168.
06

Lowering the false-alarm probability to 0.01 makes half the alarms true

The two terms of the denominator in 8.7 are the share of the crowd that sets off the alarm truly, η1r, and falsely, η0(1 − r). The notes point out that when r is small compared with η0 the second is the larger. At r = 0.01 it is 0.0495, five times the first, 0.0099.

Cutting η0 to 0.01 makes the false term 0.0099, equal to the true one, so P(R | G) = 0.0099/(0.0099 + 0.0099) = 0.500. In 10 000 people there are 99 true alarms and 99 false.

The alarms in 10 000 people at r = 0.01 and η1 = 0.99, for η0 = 0.05 and η0 = 0.01.

Key idea. With rare sources, the quiet of the background sets how far an alarm can be trusted, far more than the detection probability does.
See itSet η0 to 0.01 and send a crowd of 10 000 through. Watch for: from a source reading 99, no source (false) reading 97, and fraction from a source 0.505, close to the dashed line at 0.500.
07

When more people carry a source, the same arch gives mostly true alarms

Dividing the top and bottom of 8.7 by η0(1 − r) writes it as odds:

The odds that an alarm is true are the prior odds that a person carries a source, times the ratio η1/η0.

At η1 = 0.99 and η0 = 0.05 the ratio is 19.8 for every r. At r = 0.01 the prior odds are 0.0101, so the odds are 0.2 and P(R | G) = 0.167. At r = 0.2 and η0 = 0.01 the ratio is 99 and the prior odds 0.25, so the odds are 24.75 and P(R | G) = 0.961.

08

Summary

In one line. This sim sends a crowd through a monitor arch that sounds with one probability for carriers of a source and another for everyone else, and follows the fraction of the alarms that come from a source.

Key points

  • P(R | G) = η1r/[η1r + η0(1 − r)] is the share of alarms from a source. It is not η1.
  • The crowd size narrows the run-to-run scatter, as 1/√A, but leaves P(R | G) unchanged.
  • Lowering η0 or raising r lifts P(R | G). Raising η1 to 1 barely does.

Common mix-ups

  • "The arch catches 99 % of sources, so 99 % of alarms are real." 99 % is P(G | R). At r = 0.01 and η0 = 0.05, only 9.9 of 59.4 alarms are real.
  • "A 5 % false-alarm rate means 5 % of alarms are false." It means 5 % of the people with no source set it off. Five alarms in six are false here.
  • "A perfect detector makes every alarm real." At η1 = 1 the share is 0.168.
  • "A bigger crowd makes each alarm more trustworthy." It only tightens the scatter around 0.167.

Things to try on your own

  • Set r to 0.05, keep η1 = 0.99 and η0 = 0.05, run a crowd of 10 000, and compare the end of the curve with the dashed line at 0.510.
